author.name: Rizwan Shaikh
author.bio: I lead the content team at Dynamic Dreamz, shaping clear, purposeful narratives across blogs, landing pages, and brand communication. With a strong grasp of SEO, storytelling, and buyer intent, I focus on creating content that’s not just readable but also useful, relevant, and built to drive real business outcomes.

children: Most people think that Shopify B2B pricing is one setting, but it’s not; it’s a structure. Different buyers require different rates, different minimums, and sometimes fully negotiated terms. Hence, it’s quite important to get the structure right, and pricing runs itself. Get it wrong, and you’re manually overriding prices every time an order comes in. Here’s how to actually set it up.

content: An exact price per product or variant, assigned to a specific catalog. This is the simplest approach and works well when you have clearly defined buyer tiers with stable pricing.
A flat markdown off your standard retail price, applied to a customer group or catalog. Easier to maintain as your product line grows, since you’re not re-entering fixed prices for every new SKU.
Price decreases as order quantity increases, common for genuinely bulk-driven wholesale relationships where volume is the main lever.

children: Custom rates for individual high-value accounts, often used alongside one of the above as an exception layer rather than the default structure.

children.text: Most stores end up using a combination:

children: a base tiered structure for most wholesale buyers, with negotiated exceptions for a handful of key accounts.

Catalogs are what connect pricing to specific buyers. Assign a catalog to a company or location, then set pricing inside it; this is how the same product can show three different prices to three different buyer types without any manual intervention at checkout.

start with one catalog and a simple structure, then split into more catalogs as distinct buyer segments emerge, rather than over-engineering the structure before you have real order data. If you want, you can get help from an experienced

Shopify’s built-in B2B pricing tools, catalogs, fixed prices, quantity rules, and percentage discounts cover most standard wholesale pricing needs well. If your Shopify customer-specific pricing logic fits into “different price for different buyer group” or “discount increases with quantity,” native functionality will likely handle it without extra development.
Native tools start to strain in specific situations:

content: that changes based on factors Shopify doesn’t natively track, like real-time cost inputs or contract-specific formulas
where a negotiated price needs sign-off before it takes effect
like an ERP that owns the actual price logic and needs to push updates into Shopify automatically

content.text: Very high volumes of distinct price points

content: across many accounts, where managing everything through the standard catalog interface becomes operationally heavy

children: If you’re finding yourself needing a spreadsheet or a developer to manually patch pricing exceptions every week, that’s usually the signal that custom logic, not more manual catalogs, is the right fix.

content: Start with one simple catalog and a single pricing structure
Add tiered or quantity-based pricing once you understand real order patterns
Layer in negotiated exceptions for specific high-value accounts
Only move to custom development once you hit a genuine native limitation, not before
Showing retail prices anywhere near wholesale catalog pages; this creates confusion and undermines trust in your Shopify wholesale pricing structure
Building overly complex catalog structures before you have enough real buyers to justify them
Manually overriding prices repeatedly instead of recognizing the pattern as a sign your structure needs to change

children: Good B2B pricing isn’t about offering every possible pricing model. It’s about matching the simplest structure that fits how your actual buyers operate, and knowing exactly when that structure has outgrown what native Shopify can do.
